scope: Prepare before ordinary sick days or an explicitly mentioned planned recovery. Care access and everyday logistics, not clinical decisions or emergency response.
provenance: Assistant-authored, researched candidates. Not live catalog entries, professionally reviewed advice or recorded OpenAI API outputs. Textual fit rules require implementation before automated selection.

learning_mix.note: Founder requests roughly 30-50% dedicated learning tasks, especially in tiers 2 and 3. This draft has 12/30 (40%), all among the 27 non-parked candidates (44.4%). Ten learning tasks are in tiers 2/3. Count the main completion outcome: usable knowledge, a distinction or resource awareness; practical preparation can also involve research. This is an editorial pool balance, not a quota per user or batch. Learning can earn ordinary chosen-task completion without a quiz, external contact, purchase or rehearsal; it does not prove safety or an available arrangement.

priority_review.basis: Editorial judgments using recurring needs, practical impact and value of preparing ahead. Each task's source_ids support its subject or route, not a validated comparative ranking. Use_when and skip_when still control fit; current needs can override a default band.
priority_review.scope_note: The three work/business tasks are retained and classified for completeness, but excluded from default checkbox suggestions after the work/study choice was removed. Consider only for an explicit supported request after content and integration review. SC25 is a conditional source of practical/pet-care help, not a restored work checkbox. No runtime ranking, task approval or deployment is implied.

question: What would you like to have figured out before a sick day?
helper_text: Choose what matters to you. We'll start with a few useful options.

concerns.label: Where to get care, and what it might cost
Getting food, prescriptions and everyday essentials
Making things easier at home while I rest
Having my pet cared for if I can't do the usual routine
Keeping work or study manageable if I need time off
Finding practical help or someone to check in with

manual_input.label: Anything specific you'd like help with?
manual_input.placeholder: For example: I have a cat, no nearby help, and want to prepare without booking anything yet.

priority.reason: Establishes a missing first route to care, including access and cost, without assuming an existing doctor.
priority.adjust_when: Offer for an explicit care-access gap. If a suitable route already exists, skip rather than add a second provider by default.

tasks.title: Find a care option you can actually start with
tasks.summary: You don't need a regular doctor to explore your options. Start with one route that fits your coverage and budget.
steps: With insurance, look for virtual care in your plan or benefits portal. Without a suitable benefit, try HRSA's health-center finder.
Ask one service: 'Can a new patient in my state have a virtual first visit, and what would it cost?'
Check how to request that first visit. Keep the entry page and the answer; if you contacted the service, wait for its reply.
tasks.done_when: One first-visit route has confirmed new-patient access and cost information. An unanswered inquiry is still pending.
tasks.use_when: She wants an initial care route and has not already established a suitable one. US service variant only.
tasks.skip_when: A suitable care route already exists, or the current request asks for symptom assessment or immediate care.
tasks.new_value: Discover an entry point without presuming an existing doctor; learn whether it is usable before relying on it.
tasks.cost: Research only; future care may cost money. No account, booking or subscription required by this task.
tasks.variants: If explicitly interested in self-pay virtual care, use a reviewed pay-per-visit provider and check current first-patient eligibility and total cost. If uninsured and cost-sensitive, start with the health center. These are variants of one outcome, not extra tasks.
tasks.waiting: Provider reply if details are not published.

priority.reason: Establishes in-person access when that specific route is missing; a map listing alone does not establish access.
priority.adjust_when: Use when she asks for in-person access or identifies that gap. Do not pair with SC01 merely to fill the batch.

tasks.title: Know where an in-person visit could start
tasks.summary: An online option doesn't answer every access question. If you want an in-person route too, check one clinic before you need it.
steps: Use your insurer's provider directory, or HRSA's finder without suitable coverage, to locate a nearby clinic accepting new patients.
Check whether first visits need advance registration and whether appointments or walk-ins are offered. Ask about your likely visit charge.
Confirm the clinic's address and booking route directly. Leave questions pending until answered; you don't need to book today.
tasks.done_when: You know one clinic's new-patient process, location and cost information for a future nonurgent visit.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly wants an in-person route and lacks one, or has an established virtual route with an identified in-person access gap.
tasks.skip_when: Her existing clinic already meets this need. Do not add alongside SC01 merely to fill a batch.
tasks.new_value: Find out whether a clinic can actually accept her, rather than treating a map result as access.
tasks.cost: Research free; appointment costs vary.
tasks.variants: For insured users, replace the finder with their own plan directory. No AI judgment about which symptoms belong at which facility.
tasks.waiting: Clinic or insurer reply.

priority.reason: Makes a prospective care route more dependable through understanding its access requirements and support options.
priority.adjust_when: Move first when technology or accessibility is her stated uncertainty. Actual technical failure needs problem-solving, not another reading task.

tasks.title: Know how your first video visit will work
tasks.summary: A joining link isn't the whole picture. Learn what support is available so you can choose a setup that suits you.
steps: Use HHS's telehealth guide to learn about joining instructions, captions and technical support.
Read your chosen provider's joining page. Look for browser or app requirements and how accessibility help is requested.
Find its help route if video fails. A phone alternative depends on the provider; no practice appointment or installation is needed today.
tasks.done_when: You understand the joining requirements and where to ask about support or an alternative.
tasks.use_when: She is considering or has chosen virtual care and wants to understand its technology or accessibility requirements.
tasks.skip_when: She already knows and uses the setup successfully, or has an actual connection problem requiring specific technical support.
tasks.new_value: Learn how to evaluate virtual-visit access without rehearsing an appointment merely to earn completion.
tasks.cost: Reading is free; no account, app installation or appointment required.
tasks.waiting: None for learning. An unconfirmed alternative remains a question, not established access.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Joining requirements, accessibility support and fallback options are provider-specific; know where to find them before relying on video.

priority.reason: Closes a missing transport route that can make otherwise available nonurgent care inaccessible.
priority.adjust_when: Only offer for a stated transport gap. Use confirmed eligibility, and keep emergency transport and procedure escorts separate.

tasks.title: Find a way to an appointment without driving
tasks.summary: Some transport options need advance notice. Find out what you could use before the day you need a ride.
steps: If you have Medicaid, ask your plan about nonemergency medical transport. Otherwise, ask the clinic or local 211 about suitable transport options.
Ask one provider about eligibility, booking notice and the full return-trip cost. Mention any access assistance you actually need.
Check how the journey home is arranged, especially if the appointment runs late. Keep a confirmed booking route; don't reserve a trip yet.
tasks.done_when: You have an eligible transport option with confirmed booking and return-trip details. An unanswered inquiry is still pending.
tasks.use_when: She identifies a nonurgent appointment-transport gap. Medicaid route requires confirmed enrollment; local 211 route is US-specific.
tasks.skip_when: Transport is already arranged, she needs emergency transport, or this is an escort requirement after a procedure.
tasks.new_value: Discover possible transport assistance and its advance-booking and return-trip conditions.
tasks.cost: Research free; eligibility and ride charges vary. Do not promise free rides.
tasks.waiting: Transport-provider eligibility confirmation.

priority.reason: Resolves a potentially blocking escort arrangement before an explicitly planned procedure.
priority.adjust_when: Only eligible when a planned procedure and possible escort gap are explicit. Never make this a routine sick-day starting task.

tasks.title: Check what 'someone to take you home' really means
tasks.summary: For a planned procedure, a ride and an approved escort can be different things. Let the clinic explain what your appointment requires.
steps: Ask your procedure team who may accompany you home and whether someone must stay afterward. Use their instructions for your appointment.
If you have no suitable person, say so now. Ask the clinic's coordinator about acceptable arrangements and any referral or cost information.
Have the team confirm that your proposed arrangement meets its requirements before relying on it. Keep unresolved care needs with the team.
tasks.done_when: Your procedure team has confirmed an acceptable arrangement. An unresolved gap or a ride booking alone isn't completion.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly mentions a planned procedure or recovery with a possible escort requirement.
tasks.skip_when: Ordinary sick-day preparation with no planned procedure. Never infer a procedure from living alone.
tasks.new_value: Learn an easily missed requirement before an appointment is disrupted; access the clinic's coordination help.
tasks.cost: Planning free; acceptable transport or support may cost money.
tasks.waiting: Clinical team and prospective escort confirmation.

priority.reason: Improves a care decision by explaining the scope and limits of cost information.
priority.adjust_when: Move first when pricing uncertainty is the current barrier. This learning task does not establish affordability or supply a personalized estimate.

tasks.title: Learn what a care estimate leaves out
tasks.summary: A quoted visit price may not explain every charge. Learn what to ask before deciding about a planned self-pay visit.
steps: For US care paid without insurance, read CMS's explanation of a good faith estimate.
Notice that an estimate can cover one provider or facility; other providers and separately scheduled services may need separate estimates.
Identify the question you'd ask before booking: 'Which providers or services aren't included?' Keep the official guide if useful.
tasks.done_when: You understand what an estimate covers, its limits and how to request one.
tasks.use_when: She is exploring or planning nonemergency US self-pay care and does not understand written estimates.
tasks.skip_when: She already understands estimates, is using insurance for this visit, or needs immediate care. Do not delay needed care for research.
tasks.new_value: Gain the knowledge to question an incomplete headline price without needing a booking or a new quote today.
tasks.cost: No purchase or booking.
tasks.waiting: None for learning; obtaining an actual personalized estimate is a separate action.
tasks.learning_takeaway: An estimate is not necessarily the whole bill: separate providers and services can require separate estimates.

priority.reason: Establishes a missing way to receive a prescription without going out, including real pharmacy restrictions.
priority.adjust_when: Only when prescription access is relevant and unresolved. Existing reliable delivery makes this redundant; this never selects medication.

tasks.title: Find out whether a pharmacy can reach your door
tasks.summary: A new prescription and a routine mail-order refill can have different delivery arrangements. Check the route you might actually need.
steps: Choose a local pharmacy from your plan's directory, if insured, or an official pharmacy site. You don't need an existing prescription today.
Ask whether eligible new prescriptions can be delivered to your area, the cutoff time after they're ready, and the full delivery charge.
Check how delivery is requested and received. Keep the route if workable; confirm eligibility for any actual prescription with the pharmacy later.
tasks.done_when: You understand the pharmacy's delivery process and restrictions. Eligibility for an actual future prescription still needs checking.
tasks.use_when: She lacks a workable prescription-acquisition route or asks specifically about delivery. US linked example only.
tasks.skip_when: Delivery already works for her, or she asks which medication to obtain.
tasks.new_value: Discover local prescription delivery without assuming a regular pharmacy, and distinguish it from slower refill shipping.
tasks.cost: Research only; delivery and prescriptions may cost money.
tasks.waiting: Pharmacy response; no ordering or transfers now.

priority.reason: Makes an existing medication-access process easier to navigate by explaining a common administrative distinction.
priority.adjust_when: Offer for an explicit knowledge gap. A real delay requires the pharmacy's help, not a general lesson instead.

tasks.title: Understand why a refill might need another step
tasks.summary: Refill and renewal don't mean the same thing. Knowing the difference makes pharmacy messages easier to understand.
steps: Open your pharmacy's refill help page. CVS's refill FAQ is one example explaining refill and renewal requests.
Learn the difference: an expired prescription or no remaining refills may require renewal rather than another routine refill.
Find your pharmacy's help route for a stalled request. Follow professional guidance for your prescription; keep your medication routine unchanged.
tasks.done_when: You understand refill versus renewal and know where to ask if a request stalls.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly uses an ongoing prescription and is unsure about refill or renewal messages.
tasks.skip_when: No ongoing prescription is known, the process is already understood, or the request concerns a current missed dose or medication decision.
tasks.new_value: Recognize an administrative distinction and a support route without making a practice refill request or creating another reminder.
tasks.cost: No purchase or account access needed for public guidance.
tasks.waiting: None for learning. This does not confirm eligibility, timing or availability of an actual refill.
tasks.learning_takeaway: A refill uses an existing prescription's remaining authorization; a renewal can need the prescriber. The actual pharmacy explains individual requirements.

priority.reason: Makes a possible collection route understandable before someone relies on it.
priority.adjust_when: If she needs an actual pickup or has no feasible helper, respond to that practical gap instead of offering this as arranged support.

tasks.title: Learn how prescription collection by someone else works
tasks.summary: Someone else may be able to collect for you, but the pharmacy's requirements matter. You can understand the option without arranging a favor today.
steps: Read HHS's explanation of prescription collection by a friend or family member; the pharmacist uses professional judgment.
Look for your pharmacy's pickup rules. Check identification, payment and prescription-specific restrictions rather than assuming another person can simply arrive.
Decide whether this route could be useful if a trusted willing person is available. Keep unclear requirements as questions for the pharmacy.
tasks.done_when: You understand the potential route, its limits and which pharmacy requirements still need confirmation.
tasks.use_when: She wants to understand third-party pharmacy collection as a possible route; an existing helper is not required just to learn.
tasks.skip_when: She already knows the rules, explicitly has no interest in this route, or needs a confirmed collection now.
tasks.new_value: Learn an available type of help without asking someone to demonstrate support or claiming a helper is arranged.
tasks.cost: No purchase or collection request.
tasks.waiting: None for learning. Actual collection still needs a willing suitable person and pharmacy confirmation.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Permitted collection is not guaranteed collection; the pharmacy's requirements and a suitable person's agreement matter separately.

priority.reason: Establishes usable food access by checking actual delivery cost, handoff and substitutions.
priority.adjust_when: Offer for an untested or unsuitable route. If future paid delivery is ruled out, use an eligible community or agreed-help route instead.

tasks.title: See whether groceries can reach your actual door
tasks.summary: Delivery coverage is only the start. The useful question is whether the cost and handoff would work on a day you need rest.
steps: Check your usual grocer's delivery page for your address. If it doesn't deliver, inspect one local alternative without buying a membership.
Preview a realistic small order. Check the final fees and minimum, then confirm whether the handoff is at your door or building entrance.
Check what happens when an essential item is unavailable. Save a workable option or ask support to resolve the specific obstacle; don't check out.
tasks.done_when: You understand one service's total order cost, delivery location and substitution options well enough to decide whether it fits.
tasks.use_when: Grocery delivery is untested or there is an explicit cost, access or substitution problem.
tasks.skip_when: She already has a reliable suitable service. If no-spend includes future paid services, prefer SC11 or an agreed existing helper.
tasks.new_value: Expose minimum-order charges, building handoffs and substitutions before relying on delivery.
tasks.cost: No test purchase; future food and service costs must fit her budget.
tasks.variants: If she explicitly uses EBT, explain that provider fees may need another payment method and inspect that service's current terms. Do not collect benefit information just to personalize.
tasks.waiting: Support reply if the delivery location or fees are unclear.

priority.reason: Explores a food-access route when affordability or access makes commercial delivery unsuitable.
priority.adjust_when: Give priority when the food-access constraint is explicit. Do not infer hardship or promise local eligibility or delivery.

tasks.title: Find food help without a delivery budget
tasks.summary: When food costs are the obstacle, another shopping app may not help. A local food program is a different route worth checking.
steps: Use Feeding America's finder to reach your local food bank and ask about a nearby pantry or meal program for temporary help.
Check who can use it, opening times and what a first visit requires. Say if transport or collecting food is the obstacle.
Ask whether delivery or collection by someone else is available there. Keep the confirmed access route; if it doesn't fit, ask for another referral.
tasks.done_when: You have a confirmed local food option and a workable way to receive it. Unanswered referrals are still pending.
tasks.use_when: She explicitly identifies food affordability or lack of paid-delivery access. US only for the linked route.
tasks.skip_when: No affordability/access concern is expressed. Do not infer financial hardship from living alone or lack of insurance.
tasks.new_value: Discover temporary community food support and check whether she could actually receive it.
tasks.cost: Directory research free; program terms vary. Do not promise free home delivery.
tasks.waiting: Local program reply. No eligibility promise.

priority.reason: Makes a food-access choice more dependable by distinguishing service formats and commitments.
priority.adjust_when: Offer when choosing a format is the actual gap. Do not displace affordable food access with a comparison of subscriptions.

tasks.title: Choose meal delivery that actually removes cooking
tasks.summary: A meal kit can still leave you chopping and washing up. Learn which kind of delivery removes the part you actually want help with.
steps: Compare a meal kit such as HelloFresh with prepared meals such as Factor: ingredients to cook versus meals to heat.
Check equipment needed, minimum order, recurring charges and the deadline to skip a delivery. Your usual grocer may also sell prepared meals.
Choose a format that fits your energy and budget; no order or subscription needed. If paid delivery doesn't fit, rule it out.
tasks.done_when: You understand the formats and have chosen one to explore, or ruled paid delivery out.
tasks.use_when: She is curious about meal services or wants less cooking and is open to learning about paid options. US provider examples.
tasks.skip_when: Paid services are explicitly excluded, suitable low-effort meals already work, or the actual gap is food affordability rather than service knowledge.
tasks.new_value: Distinguish food arriving from cooking being removed, and understand recurring commitments before subscribing.
tasks.cost: Browsing is free. Commercial services may involve recurring payment and minimum orders.
tasks.variants: A freezer meal is an alternative within this outcome, not a second task called 'prepare soup'. No dietary prescriptions.
tasks.waiting: None; no sample meal, trial order or subscription.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Meal kits and prepared meals remove different work. Look past promotions to preparation effort and recurring commitments.

priority.reason: Reduces repeated trips and awkward reach once the essential options are in place.
priority.adjust_when: Move first when reach or repeated getting up is her actual barrier to using essentials. Never default to rearranging an already-working space.

tasks.title: Make your resting spot work for you
tasks.summary: Try the setup from where you'll actually sit or lie down. You'll notice more than you do while standing beside it.
steps: Sit in your usual resting spot and try reaching your drink, tissues and phone. Test the charger from that position.
Move what you keep getting up for onto an existing stable surface. Keep liquids away from electrical equipment and cables out of walkways.
Try it again, including getting up normally. Keep only changes that make reaching things and moving around easier.
tasks.done_when: Your chosen essentials are reachable and the setup leaves a clear way through.
tasks.use_when: She reports repeated getting up, awkward reach or an unsuitable resting space, or explicitly wants a simple physical preparation.
tasks.skip_when: The setup already works. Do not use this familiar task as the default for someone asking for overlooked services.
tasks.new_value: Test usability rather than collecting more objects or purchasing an emergency basket.
tasks.cost: No purchase; rearrange existing ordinary items.
tasks.waiting: None.

priority.reason: Removes a known last-minute shopping inconvenience without inventing a stockpile or universal shopping list.
priority.adjust_when: Treat as core when the specific missing item is necessary for her stated daily needs and replacing it is feasible. Respect no-purchase constraints.

tasks.title: Take one last-minute shop off your future plate
tasks.summary: Think of the everyday item that has actually sent you out at an inconvenient time. Prepare for that gap, instead of buying a generic sick-day kit.
steps: Pick a nonmedical essential you regularly use and have run out of, such as tissues, menstrual products or pet litter.
Check what you have and its storage instructions. If useful and affordable, add a modest spare to your next normal shop.
Place the spare where you'll use it and add a replacement to your shopping list when you open it. Use your existing system.
tasks.done_when: That specific supply gap is covered and you have a simple cue to replace it when used.
tasks.use_when: She describes a recurring shortage or explicitly wants material preparation; the item must come from her own routine.
tasks.skip_when: Adequate supplies already exist, buying anything is not feasible, or the request concerns medication quantities.
tasks.new_value: Close an actual recurring shortage rather than prescribe a stockpile. Lower priority for users seeking unfamiliar options.
tasks.cost: May require a routine purchase; never recommend stockpiling or automatic subscriptions.
tasks.waiting: Next ordinary shop, if needed.

priority.reason: Strengthens everyday food decisions with a reusable source and the knowledge to match its guidance.
priority.adjust_when: Prioritize a stated storage knowledge gap. Do not make it general homework or provide AI food-safety clearance.

tasks.title: Find a reliable answer to food-storage questions
tasks.summary: You don't have to memorize storage rules. Learn where to find guidance for the food you actually use.
steps: Open USDA's FoodKeeper website or app and look up one food whose storage instructions you find unclear.
Find the matching form and storage conditions, then compare the guidance with the product's packaging instructions.
Identify where you'd check again after opening or preparing that food. Use the matching entry and packaging instructions rather than a broad rule.
tasks.done_when: You can find storage guidance matching that food and know where to look again.
tasks.use_when: She wants a reliable food-storage reference or is uncertain about guidance for a familiar food.
tasks.skip_when: She already knows and uses a suitable reference, or asks whether a particular questionable food is safe to eat.
tasks.new_value: Build a reusable research skill rather than make someone prepare a portion solely to demonstrate learning.
tasks.cost: No purchase; the official web reference is enough.
tasks.waiting: None. Do not treat a lookup as clearance that a particular food is safe.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Storage guidance depends on the food and its condition; a trusted lookup tool is more useful than a universal rule.

priority.reason: Builds awareness of an optional service that can remove carrying and laundry effort.
priority.adjust_when: Move first when access or lifting is a real barrier. If she needs service now, help locate a feasible option rather than stop at general learning.

tasks.title: Decode a laundry pickup service's real cost
tasks.summary: A per-pound price isn't always what a small load costs. Learn which terms matter before relying on pickup laundry.
steps: Explore Poplin or a local laundromat's pickup page to see how collection, washing and return work in your area.
Look beyond the advertised rate: check minimum charges, additional fees, turnaround and whether detergent preferences or certain items have restrictions.
Identify which terms would decide whether the service fits your needs. Stop at understanding the option; no trial load or booking.
tasks.done_when: You understand the charging model and the service terms you would check before ordering.
tasks.use_when: She wants to learn about laundry help and is open to a possible future paid service.
tasks.skip_when: Laundry support is already understood, paid help is ruled out, or the need involves items the ordinary service will not accept.
tasks.new_value: Discover pickup laundry and learn to read its terms without carrying out an artificial trial.
tasks.cost: Research free; future service costs vary.
tasks.waiting: None for learning; exact availability and final charges still need checking before a real order.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Minimums and additional charges can matter more than a low unit price, especially for a small load.

priority.reason: Improves decisions about optional household help by explaining the terms that affect fit.
priority.adjust_when: Prioritize when misunderstanding scope is the stated obstacle. A pressing household need may require finding actual help instead.

tasks.title: Understand what a cleaning booking actually includes
tasks.summary: A cleaning listing doesn't tell the whole story. Learn how to spot the difference between a good fit and a booking that leaves your main chore untouched.
steps: Look at Taskrabbit's cleaning overview or a local cleaner's service list. Find whether your particular chores appear in the advertised scope.
Check hourly versus fixed pricing, minimum booking, supplies and exclusions. A listed hourly rate alone doesn't tell you the total.
Identify the two details you would clarify before booking. You can finish without requesting quotes, arranging a visit or sharing home-access information.
tasks.done_when: You know how to check whether a cleaning service includes the work you actually need.
tasks.use_when: She is exploring cleaning help and is unsure how to read service scope and pricing.
tasks.skip_when: She already understands the relevant service or excludes paid help. Do not substitute a cleaner for personal or clinical care.
tasks.new_value: Learn to judge a service listing and ask useful questions, without requiring a conversation or booking to count as progress.
tasks.cost: No purchase or quote request.
tasks.waiting: None for learning; no particular cleaner's cost or suitability is confirmed.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Service scope, charging method and supplied equipment affect whether a cleaning booking solves the actual need.

priority.reason: Creates a practical outside-help route for an identified errand that cannot reasonably wait.
priority.adjust_when: Only offer for a real unresolved nonmedical errand. Do not invent an errand, a nearby friend, affordable paid help or guaranteed community assistance.

tasks.title: Find help for an errand you can't postpone
tasks.summary: Some errands fall outside grocery delivery. Start with the exact job, then look for a service or local program that handles it.
steps: Choose one nonmedical errand, such as collecting a repaired item. For paid help, try Taskrabbit; for community options, contact local 211.
Ask about that exact job, area, notice and total charges. If collection is involved, check the shop's permission or identification requirements.
Keep one suitable contact and its booking process. If no service fits, leave the gap open rather than treating a directory as arranged help.
tasks.done_when: A provider has confirmed it can handle that kind of errand and explained how you would arrange it.
tasks.use_when: An identified nonmedical errand needs outside help. Choose the paid or community route from her preferences; linked coverage is US-first.
tasks.skip_when: The errand already has a solution, it is medication collection, or she needs hands-on personal care.
tasks.new_value: Convert an overlooked errand into a checked service option without assuming nearby friends.
tasks.cost: Research free; paid and community routes have different terms. A referral is not a guarantee of free assistance.
tasks.waiting: Service or referral response.

priority.reason: Establishes wanted social support through an actual mutual arrangement rather than an assumed available contact.
priority.adjust_when: Only when she wants connection and has a suitable person she is comfortable asking. Skip for someone who prefers quiet; this is not monitoring.

tasks.title: Make a check-in something you both want
tasks.summary: A short chat can be welcome without becoming another obligation. Set it up with someone you already feel comfortable asking.
steps: Choose a person you'd like to hear from on a sick day. They don't need to live nearby.
Ask what would suit you both: a message, short call or voice note, and a reasonable time. Make declining or rescheduling easy.
Agree how you'd ask for a check-in and let each other know if plans change. Keep it flexible.
tasks.done_when: You both agree on a comfortable way to arrange a check-in; an unanswered message is still pending.
tasks.use_when: She wants companionship and has named or confirmed a trusted person she is comfortable asking.
tasks.skip_when: She prefers quiet, has no such contact, or wants emergency monitoring. Living alone is not evidence of loneliness.
tasks.new_value: An actual mutual arrangement that respects both people's preferences, not a contact list or assumed availability.
tasks.cost: No purchase.
tasks.waiting: The other person's reply.

priority.reason: Makes outside-help decisions more reliable by clarifying service scope before relying on a provider.
priority.adjust_when: Useful for a real service-type knowledge gap. For an actual clinical or personal-care uncertainty, the care team must guide the decision.

tasks.title: Learn which kind of home help fits
tasks.summary: Cleaning, errands and hands-on personal care are different kinds of help. Knowing the distinction gives you better words to find the right support.
steps: Read MedlinePlus's home-care overview: it separates household work, personal care such as dressing, and healthcare support.
Match the help you're exploring to that distinction. An ordinary cleaner or errand worker isn't a substitute for personal or clinical care.
Identify which service type to research next. For healthcare needs, use your care team's guidance rather than choosing care from a marketplace listing.
tasks.done_when: You understand the service types and which kind of provider to ask about your stated need.
tasks.use_when: She is exploring outside help and is unsure which type of service fits a stated practical need.
tasks.skip_when: She already knows the appropriate service, only wants companionship, or needs a professional to assess current care needs.
tasks.new_value: Replace an assumed favor arrangement with useful vocabulary and boundaries for discovering outside support.
tasks.cost: No purchase or contact required to learn.
tasks.waiting: None for learning. No provider, eligibility, clinical plan or arrangement is established.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Different support needs call for different services; the name of the task helps find suitable help and avoid relying on the wrong provider.

priority.reason: Improves future help-seeking by teaching a reusable route to relevant local resources.
priority.adjust_when: Offer for resource awareness. If she requests concrete help for a particular errand, use SC18 or a fitting action rather than repeat directory browsing.

tasks.title: Discover local help beyond people you already know
tasks.summary: You don't need a local network to start learning what support exists. In the US, 211 is one place to explore community resources.
steps: Open your local 211 website and see which support areas it covers, such as food access or transportation.
Choose one area relevant to you and read a listing's service description, eligibility and contact route where available.
Find how to reach 211 if searching is confusing. It offers information and referrals; a listing does not guarantee assistance.
tasks.done_when: You know a local starting point and how to investigate one relevant type of support.
tasks.use_when: She is in the US, wants awareness of community resources and does not already know a suitable local starting point.
tasks.skip_when: She already uses local 211, has a confirmed route for the need, is outside the resource's coverage, or needs immediate intervention.
tasks.new_value: Discover a reusable local information route without needing a willing friend, placing a practice call or arranging help today.
tasks.cost: Information and referrals are free; referred programs have their own costs and eligibility.
tasks.waiting: None for learning. Directory details need confirmation before relying on a particular service.
tasks.learning_takeaway: A local information service can help identify options beyond an existing social circle; referrals and available assistance are different things.

priority.reason: Establishes a missing process for reporting absence when that uncertainty prevents taking needed time away.
priority.adjust_when: Parked outside default suggestions after removal of the work/study choice. Consider only for an explicit supported absence-process request.

tasks.title: Find the simplest way to take a sick day
tasks.summary: Knowing the reporting process beforehand can remove a decision when you're tired. Check the rules that actually apply to your work or course.
steps: Open your workplace policy or course guidance. Find whom to notify, the required channel and when notice is expected.
If unclear, ask the responsible office about the process and any required documentation. Don't assume paid leave or a particular entitlement.
Save a short ready-to-adapt message with only required details. For example: 'I'm unwell and need to be absent today. Please confirm the next step.'
tasks.done_when: The applicable absence process is clear and your message is ready to adapt.
tasks.use_when: She works or studies, doesn't know the reporting process and wants to reduce that friction.
tasks.skip_when: She already knows the process or works for herself without an employer/course. Legal eligibility questions need jurisdiction-specific guidance.
tasks.new_value: Discover the actual notice and documentation requirements; the message is a useful byproduct, not the whole task.
tasks.cost: No purchase. This does not promise paid time off.
tasks.waiting: Workplace or course-office reply if unclear.

priority.reason: Tests whether agreed authorized cover can actually handle a time-sensitive duty without the user.
priority.adjust_when: Parked outside default suggestions. For an explicit supported request, prioritize only when a real handoff is the unresolved obstacle and cover is possible.

tasks.title: Make one work handoff usable without you
tasks.summary: Pick the responsibility that really keeps pulling you back in. A tiny tested handoff is more useful than a long document nobody can use.
steps: With your manager or teammate, choose one time-sensitive duty they can appropriately cover and confirm that they agree to take it.
Put its next action, authorized file location and decision contact in your work system. Use approved access permissions, never shared passwords.
Ask them to open the handoff and explain what they'd do first. Fix the missing information their attempt reveals.
tasks.done_when: An agreed cover person can access and use the handoff for that duty.
tasks.use_when: She has a real time-sensitive work responsibility, authorized cover is possible, and absence is difficult because information depends on her.
tasks.skip_when: No teammate or authorized cover exists, or her work is already covered. Do not pressure her to keep working while ill.
tasks.new_value: Test someone else's ability to act, rather than writing a vague absence note or duplicating known work information.
tasks.cost: No purchase.
tasks.waiting: Colleague agreement and short trial. Keep business information out of My Safety.

priority.reason: Establishes a way to pause incoming business work while identifying commitments that a platform will not pause.
priority.adjust_when: Parked outside default suggestions. Consider only for an explicit supported solo-business request with a known platform and missing pause process.

tasks.title: Find the pause button for your own business
tasks.summary: If new orders or bookings keep arriving when you're unavailable, learn what your actual platform can pause—and what still needs attention.
steps: Open the official help for your shop or booking platform. Look for vacation mode, booking availability or temporary closure.
Check whether it pauses only new work, and what happens to existing commitments, recurring fees and messages. Don't change live settings today.
Draft a customer notice and a short plan for existing commitments. Keep the official instructions ready for a future decision to pause.
tasks.done_when: You know the platform's actual pause behavior and have a plan for commitments it doesn't pause.
tasks.use_when: She runs a solo business through a named platform and needs a way to handle temporary unavailability.
tasks.skip_when: No business/platform is known, or this process already exists. No tool action to close a real shop is authorized by this preparation task.
tasks.new_value: Discover that pausing incoming work may leave existing orders and fees active; prepare for the actual limits.
tasks.cost: Research free; existing business fees may continue during a future pause.
tasks.variants: Attach ETSY_PAUSE only for an Etsy seller; another platform needs its own reviewed official instructions, not guessed controls.
tasks.waiting: None for preparation. This task never changes live business settings.

priority.reason: Can reveal a previously unknown support option for an essential practical need.
priority.adjust_when: Only with explicit benefit access and a relevant need. This is not a restored work/study checkbox or proof that personal sick leave qualifies.

tasks.title: Discover practical help hidden in your work benefits
tasks.summary: Your benefits may include more than health insurance. Learn whether practical-care support is part of your actual package, rather than assuming a provider's advertisement applies to you.
steps: Search your benefits portal for care support, dependent care or pet care. Care.com's employer care programs are an example, not proof of coverage.
Read who and which situations qualify, any registration requirement, and what you would pay. Personal sick leave may not qualify.
Decide whether a relevant benefit is documented, absent or unclear. If unclear, identify benefits support as the next contact; no inquiry is required today.
tasks.done_when: You understand the published benefit terms, or know exactly what remains unconfirmed and where to ask.
tasks.use_when: Employer benefits are explicitly known and she wants to learn about possible support for a practical or pet-care need.
tasks.skip_when: No benefit access is known, she already checked, or there is no relevant need. Employment alone does not prove benefits.
tasks.new_value: Discover potential resources and eligibility limits without making contacting HR a prerequisite to learning.
tasks.cost: No purchase. Any later benefit use may involve registration, limits or charges.
tasks.waiting: None for learning; unclear eligibility stays unconfirmed.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Provider marketing is not an employer entitlement; the actual plan's eligible situations and costs determine whether a benefit is useful.

priority.reason: Builds awareness of possible pet-care routes when the user has not known where to start.
priority.adjust_when: Once she knows the service type, help with the next real gap. An existing sitter should not trigger another app-comparison task.

tasks.title: Discover the pet-care options you could use
tasks.summary: Pet care isn't only boarding. Learn which services let your pet stay home and what you would check before choosing a sitter.
steps: Explore Rover's pet-sitting and dog-walking options. If you have a cat, also explore Meowtel's in-home cat-care services.
Compare drop-in visits, overnight care in your home, and boarding where offered. Check species, area coverage and how much time each service includes.
Choose a service type worth researching further. Check how introductions, fees and cancellations work before any future booking; no contact or payment needed today.
tasks.done_when: You understand the relevant care options and which service type you would explore next.
tasks.use_when: A pet-care interest is explicit and she wants to understand available services before choosing a carer; future paid research is welcome.
tasks.skip_when: She already understands the services and has suitable care, excludes paid options, or needs someone to care for the pet immediately.
tasks.new_value: Introduce useful apps and service differences without making a stranger meeting or relationship exercise the task.
tasks.cost: Browsing free; future care may require payment. Check current booking and introduction rules before committing.
tasks.waiting: None for learning. No sitter is vetted, available or booked by completion.
tasks.variants: Use Meowtel only for cats and where covered. For dogs, Rover is enough unless a second reviewed local resource adds value. Do not force two names or imply either is free.
tasks.learning_takeaway: Drop-ins, overnight stays and boarding are different arrangements; choose the format before investigating a particular sitter.

priority.reason: Checks a chosen carer's practical fit through an introduction and routine walkthrough rather than relying on a listing.
priority.adjust_when: Move first when a candidate exists but this is the missing step before relying on them. Do not require SC26 if she already found someone.

tasks.title: Try the pet-care handoff together
tasks.summary: A real walkthrough can reveal the detail a feeding note misses. Use it to decide whether the arrangement works for both you and your pet.
steps: Arrange an introduction with a candidate you've chosen, confirming any charge first. Stay present while they meet your pet.
Show the ordinary routine and ask them to walk through it. Capture only the details they need, including who to contact with questions.
Resolve unclear instructions and discuss how visits would be requested if you're ill, including what happens if the carer becomes unavailable.
tasks.done_when: You've met, checked the routine together and decided whether this carer fits. Future dates still need agreement.
tasks.use_when: A suitable candidate exists and an introductory visit has not happened. The user wants to take that next step.
tasks.skip_when: A trusted carer already knows the routine. Do not repeat an existing feeding note; address only a remaining handoff gap.
tasks.new_value: Move from a listing to observed practical fit; make instructions usable by another person.
tasks.cost: Meeting or trial charges may apply; ask before arranging.
tasks.waiting: Scheduling and meeting time; travel additional. Never store access codes in My Safety.

priority.reason: Closes a permission and contact gap that a chosen carer and a vet phone number alone do not resolve.
priority.adjust_when: Move first when she explicitly expects to be unavailable and this administrative arrangement is missing. Require a chosen carer and the vet's actual process.

tasks.title: Ask your vet what a pet carer would need
tasks.summary: Knowing the vet's number may not be the whole arrangement. Ask how they handle a carer's call when you aren't available.
steps: Ask your vet what permission or paperwork they use when someone else brings your pet for care and you can't immediately answer.
Discuss the decisions and payment arrangements you are comfortable authorizing. Use the practice's process rather than an AI-written legal form.
Share the agreed process with your chosen carer through a private channel, and confirm the practice has what it needs.
tasks.done_when: Your vet and chosen carer understand the permission and contact process you have agreed.
tasks.use_when: A pet and chosen carer exist, and veterinary permission during the user's absence is an unresolved concern.
tasks.skip_when: This is already arranged or the pet needs medical advice now. Do not suggest blanket authorization or unlimited spending.
tasks.new_value: Discover an administrative gap that a phone number or feeding note alone does not cover.
tasks.cost: Administrative preparation; ask about any charge. No treatment authorized by this app.
tasks.waiting: Vet-practice confirmation. Keep permissions and payment details outside My Safety.

priority.reason: Explores a potentially feasible pet-care route during an expected extended absence when commercial care is unaffordable.
priority.adjust_when: Only for an explicitly expected extended absence and affordable-care gap. Never add foster research to ordinary short sick-day preparation.

tasks.title: Explore temporary pet care when paid sitting won't stretch
tasks.summary: For an expected longer absence, some communities have temporary foster support for owned pets. Find out whether anything local fits your situation.
steps: Contact a local animal shelter or humane organization and ask about temporary care for an owned pet during a planned hospital stay or recovery.
Ask about eligibility, notice, space, duration and costs. Make clear that you are asking about temporary care, not giving up your pet.
If a program fits, ask about its written owner-caregiver agreement and return arrangements. If not, request a specific local referral.
tasks.done_when: You understand a local program's suitability and next step, or have an honest answer that this route is unavailable.
tasks.use_when: She has a pet, explicitly expects an extended absence and lacks affordable care. Local research is required; no nationwide availability promise.
tasks.skip_when: Routine short sick-day planning, no pet, or a suitable carer already exists.
tasks.new_value: Discover a possible community alternative to commercial boarding without assuming it exists or confusing fostering with surrender.
tasks.cost: Inquiry free; program eligibility, fees and capacity vary.
tasks.waiting: Local organization reply; an inquiry never establishes a placement.

priority.reason: Establishes needed help at home with the actual care team before a planned stay or procedure assumes an available helper.
priority.adjust_when: Only when planned treatment and uncertain support are explicit. Keep unresolved care requirements with the team; do not substitute a household service.

tasks.title: Help the care team understand your home situation
tasks.summary: If a hospital stay or procedure is planned, the team needs to know when there isn't someone at home to do the practical parts.
steps: Ask your procedure or hospital team who handles planning for help at home. Explain that you live alone and what help is actually available.
Discuss the daily activities you're unsure you could manage. Ask which need professional support and which could use ordinary practical help.
Request help coordinating the necessary arrangements, including costs and timing. Ask the team to confirm the plan before relying on it.
tasks.done_when: You and the care team have an agreed support plan, with unresolved arrangements clearly assigned for follow-up.
tasks.use_when: A hospital stay or procedure is explicitly planned and help at home is uncertain.
tasks.skip_when: Ordinary sick-day preparation with no planned treatment. A cleaner or errand helper must not be substituted for clinical/personal care.
tasks.new_value: Discover discharge or care-coordination support and explain the real home situation before a care plan assumes an available helper.
tasks.cost: Ask about coordination and service costs; eligibility and coverage vary.
tasks.waiting: Team coordination; 25 minutes is active discussion/preparation, not total arrangement time.
